prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, from the magic-wavelength concept to fractional uncertainties near 10^-18, opening new tests of fundamental physics

statement.case_for: I keep B036 as my single-part first choice; my preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1 (B036, Katori and Ye), and what has changed is how firmly I hold it. The chair asked me, as the member who ranked it lowest at opening, whether the Kroll and Lindroth answer settles my objection. On the physics it does. A frequency comb is a ruler for optical cycles, and the 2012 prize concerned quantum control of single trapped particles. Neither delivered a many-atom clock whose accuracy is set by the atom and not by the trap. The magic-wavelength condition is a precise statement about the polarisabilities of the two clock states, and it is what lets thousands of atoms be interrogated at once with the trap perturbation cancelled. That is a new regime of control over a quantum system, not a polish of earlier metrology. Independent reproduction at JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, NIST, PTB and SYRTE, with fibre and free-space comparisons, answers my robustness question. The consequences are fundamental: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, limits on drifts of constants, and ultralight dark-matter searches. The pending redefinition of the second affects timing at most, not merit or attribution, so I would not wait for it. I would write the citation around the lattice concept and the 10^-18 regime so it does not read as a continuation of the comb or ion-clock citations.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 single-quantum-system prize is reduced for me but not gone, since some colleagues will still read a clock prize as an extension of honoured metrology, and the committee should be able to say in one sentence why it is not. The attribution record is the second concern. Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, and the PTB, NIST, SYRTE and RIKEN groups lie outside a Katori and Ye pairing. I am a theorist from outside atomic metrology and cannot settle the priority history from the supplied names, and the rest of us are mostly working from recollection. I would accept the two names as the best available allocation, and I would ask an atomic-physics expert reviewer or the archival record to confirm it before the vote is final. Finally, the field's own record of instrument-led prizes means that a sceptical colleague could ask whether this is physics discovery or engineering. I think the magic-wavelength insight answers that, but it is a judgement.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the 2005 and 2012 prizes did not reward interrogating thousands of neutral atoms in a magic-wavelength lattice, which moved accuracy and stability down by about two orders of magnitude, so this is a change in what can be measured and not a polish.
responses.response: That answer settles most of my opening objection, and I say so plainly since the chair asked. A change of two orders of magnitude in uncertainty that comes from removing the trap as the limiting systematic is a change of regime. I still ask the committee to put it in the citation text and not only in the rationale. On the attribution question the chair raised, I would be uncomfortable calling Kroll's recollection and mine a sufficient record by themselves, and I would favour asking an external clock expert to confirm that Katori proposed and first realised the magic-wavelength lattice clock and Ye drove the record systematic control. I also withdraw the circuit-QED first choice from my opening ballot. Your note about Wallraff's absence stands, and it is a further reason not to advance B044.

responses.point: Lindroth builds the case on light-shift physics, saying the uncertainty is set by the atom and not the apparatus, and holds the comb and ion-clock overlap serious but not decisive. She also floats a combination with a second distinct achievement such as cold-atom lattice simulation as a more balanced alternative.
responses.response: I agree with her framing of the physics and with her view that the overlap worry is not decisive. On a combination with B046 I disagree. A second part would need Bloch, Cirac, Greiner, Zoller and Esslinger to be reduced to a handful of names within the three-person limit, and that would force exactly the allocation fights that make B036 attractive. A clean two-name single prize is stronger. I also note that you and I both work close to cold-atom and circuit platforms, and neither of us is a clock-metrology specialist, so on the finer priority history among Sr, Yb and Hg groups I would defer to an external expert.

responses.point: Mehlig argues that the discovery should be separated from the mechanism in B022, that waiting for the pairing mechanism is an unusually strict test, since cuprate superconductivity and the quantum Hall effects were recognised before they were understood, and that he would shift only if the flat-band picture itself were contested.
responses.response: This is a fair rebuttal and I revise part of my round-1 position. The magic-angle flat band is a stable and quantitatively tested prediction, and the existence of correlated insulators and superconductivity in it has been reproduced for years, so I no longer treat the open pairing mechanism as disqualifying. I keep B036 ahead for two reasons. One is maturity. The decisive experiments date from 2018, and twist-angle disorder still limits sample-to-sample reproducibility, which is the robustness test I care most about. The other is the attribution problem that you and Eriksson both concede: Cao and the other first authors cannot be named, and earlier moire band theory is a possible precursor. I would move B022 up as my first alternative, and in a few years it may well be the better prize.

responses.point: Eriksson now prefers B022 over his opening B054, argues the 2018 phases have been reproduced by many groups over eight years, and accepts B036 as the mature and broadly confirmed safer choice if the committee requires settled interpretation.
responses.response: I appreciate that you conceded the Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang point on B054, and I do not wish to reopen it. You describe B036 as a safer choice if settled interpretation is required, and my view is that it is more than that: it is the case where theory, measurement and independent reproduction line up most closely. The chair asked what would keep you or Mehlig from joining B036. If the objection is that clocks are metrology and not discovery, I would answer that the magic-wavelength lattice demonstrates controlled many-atom quantum physics at a level where gravitational redshift is resolved over millimetres. If the objection is something else, I would like to hear it. I would not oppose B022 as a later prize.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B012 for the diffuse astrophysical flux and the opening of neutrino astronomy, would accept B036 as the cleaner case if the committee wants fully settled interpretation, and acknowledges that the Baikal and DUMAND pioneers make the allocation delicate.
responses.response: I respect the diffuse-flux discovery, and I defer to him on astroparticle physics. My difficulty is the one he names: two names cannot fairly represent DUMAND, AMANDA, Baikal and a collaboration of hundreds, and source identification of TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 still rests largely on IceCube alone. His own willingness to accept B036 as the cleaner case is, for me, the most useful sign in the discussion. I have listed B012 as my second alternative this time, and I would reconsider if KM3NeT or Baikal-GVD independently confirm the source associations and the committee finds a defensible allocation.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that the lattice clock is a distinct step from the 2005 comb and 2012 single-quantum-system prizes, and whether the citation wording makes that distinction explicit.

Whether Katori and Ye are exactly the right two names given Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and the PTB, NIST, SYRTE and RIKEN contributions, which I cannot verify from the supplied record and which an external expert should confirm.
Whether the redefinition of the second should be awaited. I think not, but Kroll and Pearce have not settled this.
Whether B022 will look premature or timely in a few years, and whether B012 can find a defensible allocation among pioneers and the collaboration.
statement.conflict_note: I am director of the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and a close colleague of superconducting-circuit groups, and Chalmers hosted 2025 circuit laureates as guest researchers. I would recuse myself from any decision on B044 (circuit QED) and no longer propose it, even as an alternative. I have no tie to Katori, Ye, JILA or RIKEN, and none to B022 or B012. Olsson and I are both at Chalmers or its neighbouring environment, which I note but which does not bear on any shortlisted candidate I prefer.
